component.name: Apache Teaclave TrustZone SDK
component.description: Rust SDK for writing Arm TrustZone Trusted Applications (TAs) and Client Applications (CAs), following the GlobalPlatform TEE Internal Core API and the OP-TEE implementation it is built on. Nothing in the SDK weakens or replaces those guarantees; it provides ergonomic Rust bindings on top. optee-utee is the TA library on the trusted Secure World side; optee-teec is the CA library running in the untrusted Normal World. Individual demos (e.g. projects/web3/eth_wallet) carry their own additional security-assumptions sections not repeated in the model.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it.

blueprints.name: TrustZone two-world partition
blueprints.description: A TrustZone system is partitioned into two worlds by hardware: the Normal World (REE) runs the rich OS (Linux/Android), the CA, and all user apps and is untrusted; the Secure World (TEE) runs OP-TEE OS and Trusted Applications and is trusted. Secure World memory is not visible to the Normal World. The single most important boundary is the TA entry point: everything crossing from the Normal World into a TA is attacker-controlled until the TA has validated it.

assets.name: optee-utee (TA library)
assets.description: Boundary plus trusted code: the boundary lives here in parameter.rs, tee_parameter.rs, the entry-point glue (#[ta_invoke_command], #[ta_open_session] macros), and any unsafe dereference of caller-supplied pointers/lengths. ParamMemref::buffer() constructs a Rust slice directly over the Normal-World-supplied pointer and size; OP-TEE core guarantees the pointer refers to memory the caller may share, but the contents and length are attacker-chosen and the backing memory remains mapped and writable by the Normal World during the call.

assets.name: optee-utee-macros (entry-point codegen)
assets.description: Boundary: the generated TA_*EntryPoint wrappers must faithfully pass param_types and the raw params and propagate errors without dropping them.

assets.name: optee-teec (CA library)
assets.description: Runs in the adversary's world. 'Missing input validation' here is generally not a TA-security finding; the TA cannot trust this code regardless. Focus is memory safety and not mishandling secrets returned to the CA.

assets.name: In-TA crates processing untrusted data (secure_db, rustls_provider)
assets.description: Logic runs in the TEE but inputs (DB contents persisted via Normal World storage, bytes from a TLS peer) originate outside the TCB; the boundary invariants apply to those inputs. Deserialization of shared proto structures inside the TA is boundary code: a malicious CA can send malformed proto bytes.

assets.name: Secure storage
assets.description: Confidential and integrity-protected, but not inherently anti-rollback or highly available: OP-TEE may persist secure objects as encrypted blobs on the Normal World filesystem, where the adversary can delete or roll them back.

assets.name: TA dependency tree
assets.description: Every crate compiled into a TA runs inside the Secure World and is part of the TCB, including crypto crates (rustls, rustls-rustcrypto, ed25519-dalek, secp256k1, sha3, bip32) and serialization crates (serde/bincode). The trust boundary stops attacker input at the entry point; it does not sandbox the TA's own dependencies.

zones.name: Normal World (REE)
zones.description: Rich OS, the CA, and all user apps; untrusted, adversary-controlled up to root privileges.

zones.name: Secure World (TEE)
zones.description: OP-TEE OS and Trusted Applications; trusted.

assumptions.description: Trusted Computing Base: the hardware root of trust and TrustZone partitioning, the secure boot chain and OP-TEE OS, the Trusted Application itself once loaded and verified by OP-TEE, and the GlobalPlatform Internal Core API surface OP-TEE provides.

The adversary has full control of the Normal World including root: it can invoke any TA with arbitrary parameters, place arbitrary content in shared memory and mutate it concurrently during a call (TOCTOU), read any Normal World memory and files including encrypted secure-storage blobs, delete/withhold/replay/reorder anything stored or transmitted through the Normal World, and observe timing and other side channels.
A secure user interface (trusted display/input) is hardware-specific and not provided by this SDK; a user confirmation that round-trips through the Normal World cannot be trusted.
Cryptographic operations should use the OP-TEE/GlobalPlatform crypto API surface (crypto_op.rs, arithmetical.rs) rather than re-implementing primitives in the TA.
no-std vs std is a TCB-size decision: std mode pulls a substantially larger dependency and runtime surface into the TCB; prefer the smallest dependency set that meets the requirement.

examples/ are illustrative teaching material, not hardened production code; projects/ are reference applications with their own stated security assumptions; tests, patches, and tools are build/test-time, not runtime TCB.

threats.name: Malicious parameters at the TA entry point
threats.description: The adversary can invoke any TA, open any session, and call any command ID with arbitrary parameters: values, buffer pointers, and buffer lengths are all attacker-chosen, and every byte of a memref is adversarial (a size of 0, a huge size, or a size not matching the payload are all legal inputs; no NUL-termination, well-formedness, or non-emptiness may be assumed). Value parameters are untrusted in content but bounded and not aliased to Normal World memory; Memref parameters are the high-risk case.

threats.name: Concurrent mutation of shared memory (TOCTOU / double fetch)
threats.description: The Normal World can mutate shared-memory buffers concurrently, including during a TA call. Reading the same shared field twice and assuming it unchanged is a double fetch; MemrefInput must be treated as read-once.

threats.name: Secret leakage through Output/Inout buffers
threats.description: Anything written to an output memref becomes visible to the Normal World; secrets must never cross to the Normal World in cleartext unless the application's threat model explicitly accepts it (returning a mnemonic or key to the CA is a deliberate, documented risk where it appears in demos).

threats.name: Malformed shared-structure bytes deserialized inside the TA
threats.description: Deserialization of proto/shared message structures inside the TA is boundary code: a malicious CA can send malformed proto bytes, and in-TA crates such as secure_db and rustls_provider process data (persisted DB contents, TLS peer bytes) originating outside the TCB.

threats.name: Rollback, deletion, or withholding of secure storage
threats.description: OP-TEE may persist secure objects as encrypted blobs on the Normal World filesystem, where the adversary can delete or roll them back. Rollback of secure storage when no anti-rollback hardware (e.g. RPMB) is used is out of scope for the SDK and the responsibility of the hardware/integrator.

threats.name: Vulnerability or backdoor in a TA dependency
threats.description: A vulnerability or backdoor in a TA dependency is code execution inside the TEE with access to the TA's secrets and capabilities; the TCB includes the full transitive dependency tree of each TA. Software crypto crates perform key operations in TA-resident memory rather than a hardware crypto engine, making side-channel resistance the integrator's concern; any RNG reaching getrandom must be sourced from a TEE/hardware entropy source, never the Normal World. Build-time dependencies (proc-macros, build scripts) execute on the build host and can tamper with the generated TA binary. The repository does not currently ship a dependency-vetting policy (no deny.toml, cargo-audit/vet/supply-chain configuration, or committed lockfile policy for downstream TAs).

threats.name: Physical, side-channel, and availability attacks
threats.description: Unless a specific demo states otherwise, the SDK does not defend against physical and hardware attacks (glitching, bus probing, decapsulation), microarchitectural side channels (Spectre-class, cache timing), or denial of service from the Normal World (which controls scheduling and power). These are the responsibility of the hardware/integrator.

threats.name: Missing input validation in Client Application code
threats.description: CA code (optee-teec, host/) runs in the untrusted world; the TA must validate regardless, so CA-side validation is not a security control and 'missing input validation in the CA' is an expected non-finding. Similarly, examples are illustrative (note copy-risk patterns rather than reporting them as production vulnerabilities), unsafe in *-sys FFI crates is not a finding merely for existing, and a demo's documented and accepted risk is not a new vulnerability.

trustBoundaries.name: TA entry point trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Crossed through the entry-point macros in optee-utee, which hand the TA a Parameters struct built from the raw TEE_Param array. Params, pointers, lengths, and buffer contents are all attacker-controlled and may mutate concurrently; validate before use. OP-TEE core guarantees a memref pointer refers to memory the caller is allowed to share, so it cannot be used to read arbitrary secure memory.

controls.name: Parameter type validation primitives
controls.description: The SDK's as_value/as_memref accessors return BadParameters on a type mismatch; TA code must validate param_types first, confirm each slot is the expected type before interpreting it, and propagate the error rather than bypassing it.

controls.name: TA boundary invariants
controls.description: Obligations on TA code, not provided automatically: treat every byte of a memref as adversarial (check length, encoding, structure; never assume NUL-termination, well-formedness, or non-emptiness); bound all lengths (0, huge, or mismatched sizes are legal adversary inputs); and fail closed, returning an error (ErrorKind::BadParameters and friends) on any validation failure rather than proceeding with partially validated input.

controls.name: Copy-then-validate against TOCTOU
controls.description: Because the Normal World can mutate a shared buffer concurrently, copy untrusted input into secure memory once before validating and using it; never double-fetch a shared field; treat MemrefInput as read-once.

controls.name: Deliberate output sizing and content
controls.description: Write only what the caller is authorized to learn to Output/Inout memrefs; size outputs deliberately and set the updated size with set_updated_size.

controls.name: Hardware anti-rollback (RPMB)
controls.description: Anti-rollback for secure storage requires hardware support such as RPMB; sealing/secure storage alone does not provide freshness or availability.

controls.name: Pin and lock TA dependencies
controls.description: Commit Cargo.lock so audited versions are reproducible for production-grade TAs.

controls.name: Run cargo audit, deny, and vet
controls.description: Run cargo audit (RUSTSEC advisories), consider cargo deny to enforce licenses and ban yanked/duplicate crates, and consider cargo vet or vendoring for the subset of crates that end up in the TCB.

controls.name: Minimize the TA dependency tree
controls.description: Review new TA dependencies as TCB additions with the same scrutiny as first-party TA code; prefer no-std, since std mode pulls a substantially larger dependency and runtime surface into the TCB.

controls.name: Prefer the OP-TEE/GlobalPlatform crypto API and TEE-backed randomness
controls.description: Where the platform offers it, prefer the OP-TEE/GlobalPlatform crypto API over software crypto crates holding key material in TA RAM, and verify that any entropy path inside a TA is TEE/hardware-backed, never sourced from the Normal World.
